node.label: Geoff Eley
node.date_label: Forging Democracy (2002) · A Crooked Line (2005) · Nazism as Fascism (2013)
node.description: Historian of modern Europe and historiography whose writing reconsiders the relation between social and cultural history. Jaume Aurell reads A Crooked Line as a deliberate use of intellectual autobiography to interpret the cultural turn and its political conditions. This plural approach does not require historians to abandon social questions when studying meaning, nor does Eley’s path stand for every national historiography.

incident_edges.relationship: Scott answers Eley and Nield that they want class 'as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory', and that insisting on class forecloses other political categories: her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (2000)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Body read in full for revision 1.152 (ILWCH 57, 2000, pp. 69–75; Cambridge PDF; data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-spread.md §6.3); the abstract read for 1.147 is confirmed verbatim. Eley and Nield's essay 'will surely become an indispensable assignment in introductory graduate courses because it is synthetic in many senses' (p. 69); they 'are willing to accommodate all manner of deviations from the materialist analyses … especially what some have dubbed "the linguistic turn"', so that one 'might have punned wildly and titled the Eley/Nield essay, "Assent to Discourse"' (p. 69); 'Patrick Joyce has been expelled from the fold and Kathleen Canning is now at its center' (p. 69); 'there's a tension between Eley and Nield's desires to update the old social history by detaching it from its materialist assumptions, on the one hand, and to keep writing narratives of worker political agency, on the other' (pp. 69–70); they talk of gender 'but no mention of sex, homo- or heterosexuality, and sexual difference' (p. 70); Rancière's 1983 essay is 'an important corrective to Eley and Nield' (pp. 70–71); 'They want to define class as an effect of discourse but also as "a structural attribute of societies" as if those two were contradictory. To posit them as contradictory is to misunderstand Foucault's ideas about discourse'; 'Structures come into being through discourse: Class is one way of naming, understanding, and organizing certain forms of social inequality' (p. 71); her questions 'don't exclude class, but they don't require it either' (p. 72). Eley and Nield's reply (pp. 81–86 read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history' (p. 83), while they 'wholeheartedly applaud Scott's citation of Rancière' (p. 84). Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay) and from languages_of_class → social, which carries the debate's bearing on the field. Earlier note (1.147): Publisher abstract only (ILWCH 57, 2000, 69–75); the article body is unread. Eley and Nield's essay is marked by a tension between detaching social history from "its materialist assumptions" and continuing "narratives of working-class political agency"; "By insisting that class is still the best way of analyzing inequality and mobilizing resistance to it, the authors foreclose other possibilities for thinking about contemporary politics and for writing critical history"; her questions "don't exclude class but they don't require it either". Moderate. Distinct from edge_105 (the linguistic turn's critique of social history, citing her 1991 essay). Routing qualification, revision 1.194: the specific target is the joint Eley/Nield argument, now reachable through Eley’s individual entry. Keith Nield retains equal authorial credit in the claim and sources; the target does not imply Eley-only authorship. The mixed-critic context on edge_1169 is preserved.

incident_edges.relationship: A Crooked Line uses intellectual autobiography as a historiographical intervention, situating methods in political and personal contexts.

incident_edges.relationship: With Keith Nield, Eley challenges Scott’s portrayal of their approach as a binary choice between discourse and materialist social history, while welcoming her insistence on sexed subjectivities (2000).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary printed pp. 83–84 freshly read, with preceding context on p. 82. The reply jointly credits Eley and Nield; this personal route projects their shared intervention, not an independent Eley-only argument. Their praise for Scott’s lucidity, acknowledgment of sexuality’s importance and agreement about Rancière qualify the criticism. Existing mixed debate edge_1169 remains unchanged.

incident_edges.relationship: Eley and Keith Nield defend the gains of Languages of Class but criticize Stedman Jones for narrowing linguistic analysis to published Chartist rhetoric and excluding the social archive (2000).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Keith Nield retains equal authorial credit. Their critique accepts much of the political reinterpretation of Chartism; it challenges the restricted archive and oversynthesized public language, not linguistic analysis itself. Mixed critic edge 1159 remains unchanged.
